title: Tagatose: What It Is, How Many Calories It Has, and Why It Behaves So Much Like Sugar

seo.title: Tagatose: Calories, Blood Sugar, and How It Compares With Sugar
seo.meta_description: D-tagatose is a rare monosaccharide related to fructose with sweetness close to sugar but lower metabolizable energy. FDA recognizes 1.5 calories per gram and in 2025 announced enforcement discretion allowing exclusion from Total and Added Sugars under specified labeling conditions. Higher doses can cause GI symptoms.
seo.search_intent: Understand what D-tagatose is, how many calories it provides, how it affects glucose, why it works like sugar in baking, and how it differs from sucrose and allulose.

excerpt: D-tagatose is a rare monosaccharide closely related to fructose. It tastes much closer to sucrose than most high-intensity sweeteners, while only part is absorbed and metabolized in the conventional way. FDA recognizes an energy value of 1.5 calories per gram in the United States. Because tagatose also supplies bulk and participates in browning, it can behave more like sugar in food formulation than stevia or sucralose.
content_html:
D-tagatose is a rare sugar with sweetness close to sucrose but substantially less metabolizable energy. It is a monosaccharide and a structural epimer of fructose, sharing the same molecular formula but differing in three-dimensional arrangement.

That small chemical difference changes absorption, metabolism, and glycemic response.

Tagatose behaves more like sugar than stevia does

Tagatose is not a high-intensity sweetener. Its sweetness is close enough to sucrose that it can be used in quantities that contribute physical bulk and texture.

It also participates in Maillard browning, helping baked foods develop color and flavor.

Recipes still need adjustment because tagatose can brown quickly and can influence water binding differently from sucrose.

FDA recognizes 1.5 calories per gram

In November 2025, FDA confirmed an energy value of 1.5 kcal/g for D-tagatose, compared with 4 kcal/g for conventional sugar.

Only part of an ingested dose is absorbed in the small intestine. Much of the remainder reaches the colon for fermentation.

This is different from isomaltulose, which is slowly but almost completely digested.

The blood-glucose response is smaller

Because a substantial fraction is not rapidly converted into available glucose, tagatose generally produces a much smaller glycemic response than glucose or sucrose.

FDA also acknowledges that human studies show a different glycemic effect from traditional sugars.

A food made with tagatose can still contain flour, starch, or other sugars, so the whole carbohydrate profile matters.

U.S. labeling policy recently changed

Tagatose historically remained within sugar declarations. In 2025 FDA stated that it intends to exercise enforcement discretion allowing D-tagatose to be excluded from Total Sugars and Added Sugars and allowing 1.5 kcal/g for calorie calculation while broader rules are considered.

This is a U.S. labeling policy and should not be assumed to apply in Europe or other markets.

Regulatory treatment can differ even when the ingredient chemistry is identical.

Unabsorbed tagatose is fermented in the colon

The fraction reaching the large intestine is fermented by microbes into short-chain fatty acids, gases, and other metabolites.

This contributes to the lower available energy value.

It also explains why high single doses can cause bloating, flatulence, abdominal discomfort, or diarrhea in some people.

Tagatose and allulose are different rare sugars

Both provide fewer calories and much smaller glycemic responses than sucrose, but their metabolism is not identical.

FDA uses 0.4 kcal/g for allulose and 1.5 kcal/g for D-tagatose.

Tagatose is generally closer to sucrose in sweetness, while allulose is often described as about 70% as sweet.

Why food formulators are interested

Tagatose combines meaningful sweetness, physical bulk, browning, and lower metabolizable energy—properties that are difficult to obtain from one high-intensity sweetener.

It can appear in confectionery, dairy foods, beverages, and baked products, often blended with other sweeteners to optimize cost, sweetness, and texture.

Tagatose also behaves differently from sugar alcohols such as erythritol or maltitol. It is chemically a monosaccharide rather than a polyol, and its sweetness and browning properties are much closer to sucrose even though part of the dose escapes small-intestinal absorption.

For people choosing a sweetener mainly for baking, this functional similarity can matter more than the calorie number alone. A product that browns, caramelizes, and contributes bulk may replace sugar more convincingly in cookies or dairy desserts than an intense sweetener that supplies sweetness but almost no mass.

The tradeoff is dose-related tolerance: because unabsorbed tagatose reaches the colon, large servings can produce more GI symptoms than a very small amount of a high-intensity sweetener.

The practical rule: tagatose acts surprisingly like sugar in taste and food structure while the body metabolizes much less of it. The tradeoff is that large doses can move more carbohydrate into the colon and cause GI symptoms.

faq.question: How many calories does tagatose have?
faq.answer: FDA recognizes 1.5 calories per gram in the U.S., compared with 4 calories per gram for sucrose.

faq.question: Does tagatose raise blood sugar?
faq.answer: Its glycemic effect is generally much smaller than conventional sugar, although the complete food may contain other carbohydrates.

faq.question: Are tagatose and allulose the same?
faq.answer: No. They are different rare sugars; FDA uses 1.5 kcal/g for tagatose and 0.4 kcal/g for allulose.
